claims.text: The initial material is a homogeneous, single-phase ferromagnetic high-entropy alloy with minimal intrinsic precipitates.
Isothermal annealing at a moderately elevated temperature, such as approximately 600°C, can promote nucleation and growth of fine nonmagnetic precipitates in the alloy.
The annealing must be performed in an oxygen-free or inert environment with precise control of temperature and time for the proposed effect to hold.
The proposed effect requires a ferromagnetic-element-rich alloy in which annealing produces a nanoscale nonmagnetic second phase.
Annealing induces nanoscale precipitates both at grain boundaries and within grains.
The induced nanoscale precipitates increase the density of magnetic-domain-wall pinning centers.
Finely dispersed nonmagnetic precipitates obstruct domain-wall motion during magnetization reversal.
Obstruction by the precipitates raises the energy barrier for domain-wall movement.
Enhanced domain-wall pinning increases coercive field relative to an untreated single-phase baseline.
The heat-treated alloy will have a higher coercive field than the matched untreated alloy because nanoscale precipitates form and stabilize.
The untreated homogeneous alloy has low coercivity because it lacks significant internal microstructural barriers.
The coercivity-enhancing effect is expected only when the annealing-induced secondary phase is nonmagnetic and effectively pins domain walls.
If the precipitates or secondary phases are magnetic, the coercivity effect may be diminished or reversed.
Differences in alloy composition may alter the effectiveness of annealing-induced precipitation for increasing coercivity.
The annealing temperature, duration, and precipitate size or distribution that maximize coercivity are not yet fully determined.
Failure of the heat-treated samples to show a statistically significant coercive-field increase over untreated controls would falsify the hypothesis.
Failure to observe consistent nanoscale precipitate formation correlated with increased coercivity would falsify the proposed precipitation-mediated mechanism.
